plan: In a second-price sealed-bid auction with independent private values, bidding one's true value is a dominant strategy regardless of what other bidders do. This is because if I bid higher than my value, I risk winning and paying more than the item is worth to me; if I bid lower, I risk losing a profitable opportunity. Since I pay the second-highest bid (not my own bid) when I win, there's no incentive to shade my bid. Therefore, my optimal strategy is to bid exactly my value of $31, regardless of my beliefs about Betty and Charles's strategies.

In a second-price sealed-bid auction (winner pays second-highest bid), truthful bidding is a weakly dominant strategy regardless of other bidders' behavior. Bidding my true value ensures I win whenever my value exceeds the price I'd pay, and I never overpay since I only pay the second-highest bid, not my own bid. This holds regardless of what Andy and Charles do or think about my strategy, since the payment I make doesn't depend on my own bid (only on whether I win and what the second-highest bid is). Therefore, I should bid exactly my value of $37.

This is a second-price sealed-bid auction (winner pays second-highest bid). In such auctions, bidding truthfully (bid = value) is a dominant strategy regardless of what others do—it maximizes expected profit since you win exactly when your value exceeds the second-highest bid, and you never pay more than your value. Overbidding risks winning at a loss; underbidding risks losing profitable wins. With my value at $11, I should bid $11 exactly.
